Adams Circle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch six dots on its sides.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show or hide the guides.
Look for the math

The six dots sit on the sides of any triangle you draw. Move a corner as far as you like and they still lie on one circle — and the centre of that circle never moves away from the middle of the incircle. That was C. Adams' discovery in 1843.

Building the six points

The incircle touches the three sides at D (on BC), E (on CA) and F (on AB). The lines AD, BE and CF meet at one point, the Gergonne point G. The triangle DEF is called the contact triangle. Now draw through G a line parallel to each side of DEF. Those three lines cut the sides of ABC in six places: P and Q on BC, R and S on CA, T and U on AB. Those are the six dots.

Equal steps from the touch points

Because AE = AF (two tangents from the same point), triangle EAF is isosceles. The line through G parallel to EF makes triangle UR A similar to it, so UR is isosceles too. Comparing equal lengths gives ER = FU, and the same argument on the other sides gives DQ = FT and DP = ES.

Two midpoints finish the proof

Turn on the hint. The line through A parallel to BC meets DE and DF at X and Y, and A is exactly halfway between them. It is also halfway between M and N, where those lines meet PS and QT. Taking the two halves away leaves MX = NY; since MX = DP and NY = DQ, we get DP = DQ. Together with the pairs above, all six of DP, DQ, ER, ES, FT, FU are equal. The touch points are the feet of the perpendiculars from the incenter I, so equal steps along the sides mean equal distances from I: all six dots lie on a circle centred at I.

The logic test confirms every one of these claims on hundreds of exact and random triangles: the largest difference between the six distances is under a billionth of a drawing unit. It also checks each constructed point against a second transcription of the applet's own method.

Turn off Adams circle and guess where its centre is. Then tick the incircle: the centre you guessed is the centre of both circles. Which pair of equal steps is easiest to see when two sides are nearly the same length?
